transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving all day, going from one little job to the next, like I’ve still got a crew waiting on me or something. It’s hard for me to just sit and be still.
Along with feeling like you can't slow down, have you also noticed your mood being unusually high, euphoric, or irritable—or is it more that you feel anxious or on edge?
I don’t think it’s like a high or euphoric feeling, no. I’m not sure about irritable either. It’s more just… I feel wound up, like I can’t settle down. Maybe on edge, but not in a big dramatic way.
Did this feeling of being unable to slow down start only after you stopped working, or is this something you've noticed on and off since you were younger, even before this job change?

No, it didn’t just start after I stopped working. Looking back, it was there when I was a kid too. In grade school, teachers would say I was bright but scattered. I was always losing pencils, blurting out answers, and needing reminders to finish my work before recess.

latest_inference.note: Childhood-onset inattentive/hyperactive symptoms (losing items, blurting answers, needing reminders) with continued restlessness into adulthood support ADHD; absence of mood elevation argues against bipolar/hypomania, and lifelong pattern rather than situational onset argues against adjustment disorder or GAD.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong pattern (since grade school) of restlessness, difficulty sitting still, disorganization, losing items, blurting out answers, and needing reminders to complete tasks—classic hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms with childhood onset persisting into adulthood. Mood is described as 'wound up' rather than euphoric or classically anxious, and there is no episodic mood elevation, grandiosity, or discrete manic/hypomanic episode to suggest a bipolar spectrum disorder, nor a pervasive anxious/worry pattern to support a primary anxiety disorder. The chronic, early-onset, cross-situational nature of hyperactivity and inattentive traits best fits ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
